evals.prompt: two judges: adversarial review of the staged diff
evals.expected_output:
Judgment Day for the staged diff — two independent judges, sealed verdicts, same target material:
- Judge Red (challenger): how does this break? Failure modes, edge cases, race conditions, security holes.
- Judge Blue (advocate): how does this fail to deliver? Missing requirements, undersized scope, ambiguity that causes rework.
Both answer the same template under four headings: 1) Blocking issues 2) Likely issues 3) Blind spots 4) Verdict (SHIP / FIX / KILL).
Synthesis: overlap -> near-certain defects (blocking until proven otherwise); single-judge flags -> hypotheses to verify against the code; split verdict -> rewrite the spec/design, not the review.
Scope: post-apply / pre-PR review of the code diff; the goal is conflict surfacing.

evals.prompt: judgment day on the merge gate before the PR
evals.expected_output:
Judgment Day pre-condition guard: run only when the staged diff is >= 100 lines AND touches critical markers (auth, payments, migrations, sql, ssl, secret, jwt, bcrypt), or when the user explicitly requests it on a non-trivial change.
Below that threshold: code-reviewer only — the skill-router sets skipJudgmentDay=true for diff < 100 lines with no critical markers.
Merge gate rule: no non-trivial change merges without surviving Judgment Day (both verdicts sealed before synthesis).
Planning steps (proposal/spec/design/tasks) belong to the orchestrator gatekeeper and the phase result contract — not to the judges.
